text: Lesson 28 mapped the firms. This lesson maps the jobs inside them. "Quant" is a broad label covering at least three genuinely different roles — researcher, developer, and trader — each with a different mix of skills, and the lines between them blur more at smaller firms than at larger ones.

A quant researcher designs and tests trading signals and models — leaning heaviest on statistics, probability, and increasingly machine learning. A quant developer builds and maintains the infrastructure that research and trading actually run on — data pipelines, backtesting frameworks, execution systems — leaning heaviest on software engineering. And a quant trader executes strategies and manages risk in real time, needing market intuition and decisiveness on top of enough technical fluency to understand the models being traded.

Walk through a researcher's actual workflow and the overlap becomes clearer. It starts with a hypothesis — a suspected pattern in market data. Then comes building a model and backtesting it rigorously against history, while staying careful about overfitting to the past, since a model that fits old data too closely often fails on new data. The output gets handed off as a signal to be built into something tradeable — which is exactly where a quant developer's infrastructure and a quant trader's execution take over.

Firm size changes how distinct these roles actually are. At a large bank or an established hedge fund, researcher, developer, and trader are often separate job titles with separate reporting lines. At smaller shops, especially early-stage prop trading firms or small funds, one person frequently covers two or even all three — a researcher who writes their own production code, or a trader who builds their own execution tools. Understanding all three skill sets, even while specializing in one, makes someone more valuable across firm sizes.

Three profiles, one shared goal: turning a market idea into a well-run, well-risk-managed trade. Up next, Lesson 30: how quants get paid, building directly on the firm types and roles from this lesson and the last.
